en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Silk Cloth 17.
The Training Rule on Washing Sheep’s Wool.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Monastery.
Now at that time, the group of six monks had nuns wash, dye, and comb wool.

While washing, dyeing, and combing the wool, the nuns neglected the recitation of the scriptures, their questioning on them, and the higher training in virtue, the higher training in mind, and the higher training in wisdom.
Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī approached the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side.
As Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī was standing to one side, the Blessed One said this to her: “I hope, Gotamī, that the bhikkhunīs are dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute?
“How could there be diligence for the bhikkhunīs, Bhante?
The noble Chabbaggiyā bhikkhunīs have the bhikkhunīs wash wool, dye it, and comb it.”
“The bhikkhunīs, while washing, dyeing, and combing wool, neglect the recitation, the questioning, the higher virtue, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom.
Then the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī with a discourse on the Dhamma.

Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to her right, and departed.
Then, on this occasion and for this reason, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the group of six monks:
"Is it true, monks, that you have had wool washed, dyed, and carded by the bhikkhunīs?
"It is true, Blessed One."
“Monks, are your kinsmen unrelated to you?
“They are unrelated, Blessed One.
“Foolish men, those who are unrelated do not know what is appropriate or inappropriate, or what is inspiring or uninspiring, regarding those who are unrelated.”
In this matter, you foolish men, you will have unrelated bhikkhunīs wash, dye, and comb wool for you.
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“Whatever monk should have wool from sheep washed, dyed, or carded by an unrelated nun, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
“Whatever monk” means whichever such person... [and so forth].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"A stranger" (aññātikā) means:
Not related by mother’s side or father’s side, even back to the seventh generation of ancestors.
A “bhikkhunī” is one who has received full ordination in both Saṅghas.
If he washes it himself or orders it to be washed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Once washed, the items become subject to relinquishment (nissaggiya).
If he orders it to be dyed, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
The dyed robes become subject to forfeiture.
If she commands, "Untangle them," there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Once untangled, they become subject to forfeiture.
They are to be forfeited to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.
And thus, monks, they are to be forfeited:
…pe…
“Venerable sir, these sheep’s wool, which I had a non-related bhikkhunī wash for me, are to be forfeited.
I forfeit them to the Saṅgha. …pe… “He should give them back” …pe…
"May she give... ... [and so on] ... "I give it to the Venerable One.
If he causes wool to be washed for an unrelated woman while perceiving her as unrelated, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If he has unrelated sheep’s wool washed or dyed by an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing together with an offense entailing relinquishment.
If he has unrelated sheep’s wool washed or combed out by an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing together with an offense entailing relinquishment.

If he has unrelated sheep’s wool washed, dyed, and combed out by an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, there are two offenses of wrong-doing together with an offense entailing relinquishment.
If she causes unrelated wool to be dyed by an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and expiation (nissaggiya-pācittiya).

If she causes unrelated wool to be dyed and unbraided by an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in connection with the offense entailing relinquishment.
If she causes unrelated wool to be dyed and washed by an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing in connection with the offense entailing relinquishment.
If he has wool from an unrelated woman dyed, combed, or washed, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of expiation with forfeiture and two offenses of wrong-doing.
If he has wool from an unrelated woman combed, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of expiation with forfeiture.
If he has wool from an unrelated woman combed and washed, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing together with an offense of expiation with forfeiture.
If he has unrelated wool combed out and dyed by an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) together with the offense of relinquishment (nissaggiya).
If he has unrelated wool combed out, washed, and dyed by an unrelated woman, perceiving her as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing together with two offenses of relinquishment.
If he is in doubt regarding an unrelated woman... [and so forth].
If she is unrelated but he perceives her as related ...
[and so on] ... if he has another person wash sheep’s wool, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he has someone who is fully ordained together with him wash it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is a relative and one perceives her as not being a relative, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she is a relative and one is uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is a relative and one perceives her as a relative, there is no offense.
There is no offense if she washes while a relative is doing the washing and a non-relative is her companion,
or if she washes without being told.
If she has an un-used finished article washed by a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) or a novice nun (sāmaṇerī).
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of the first offender.
The seventh training rule concerning the washing of sheep’s wool is finished.
